s0006 names 陳矯; 矯 is Jiǎo, so Chen Qiao is a false given-name reading and Chen Jiao is the accurate replacement.
Chen Qiao's additions to the Cao offices came from military affairs to fill gaps.
Chen Jiao's additions to the Cao offices came from military affairs to fill gaps.

When the Prince of Yulin was made heir and Empress Dowager Wen'an took her honorific title, these offices were created and named after palace quarters.
When the Prince of Yulin was enthroned and Empress Dowager Wen'an took her honorific title, these offices were created and named after palace quarters.
s0156 鬱林王立 marks the prince's accession as emperor, not designation as heir; s0158 鬱林立皇后 confirms he was already reigning when the empress was installed, so enthroned is correct.

Under Wei and Jin, provincial governors were honored posts; inspectors with heavy responsibility became commissioners bearing the staff of authority and military overseers, lighter ones commissioners bearing the staff and supervisors. The office began under the Following Han emperor, when Inspector-General Feng She campaigned against Jiujiang bandits and directed Yang and Xu military affairs; but the He and Xu Song Gazetteer dates it to Cao Cao's dispatch of provincial generals to oversee troops, and Wang Guizhi's Protocol of Offices to Emperor Guangwu—all are mistaken.

Under Wei and Jin, provincial governors were honored posts; inspectors with heavy responsibility became commissioners bearing the staff of authority and military overseers, lighter ones commissioners bearing the staff and supervisors. The office began under Emperor Shun of Han, when Censor-in-chief Feng She campaigned against Jiujiang bandits and directed Yang and Xu military affairs; but He and Xu's Song Treatise dates it to Cao Cao's dispatch of provincial generals to oversee troops, and Wang Guizhi's Protocol of Offices dates it to Emperor Guangwu—all are mistaken.

Chapter 漢從帝 is a variant; CText Nan Qi shu treatises read 漢順帝 (Emperor Shun of Han). 御史中丞 is Censor-in-chief, not Inspector-General; 《宋志》 is the Song Treatise, and restoring the possessive and the verb before Emperor Guangwu matches 何、徐《宋志》…王珪之《職儀》云起光武.

In Wei and Jin times provincial governors were weighty; inspectors with heavy duty became commissioners bearing the staff of authority and overseers, lighter ones commissioners bearing the staff of authority and supervisors. It began in the time of the Following Han emperor, when Inspector-General Feng She suppressed bandits in Jiujiang and oversaw military affairs in Yang and Xu provinces; yet the He and Xu Song Gazetteer says it began when Cao Cao sent generals of the provinces to oversee armies, and Wang Guizhi's Protocol of Offices says it began with Guangwu—all are wrong.
